stages.name: Impact of demergers
stages.title: Impact of demergers
stages.sub: What happens to workers and consumers when a business splits into separate parts.

steps.q: A retail giant splits its clothing arm and its furniture arm into two separate companies. Each new company now has managers who only need to focus on one type of product. Does each part become easier or harder to run well?
steps.right: Easier, each part can concentrate on its own market
steps.wrong: Harder, each part now has fewer resources to share
steps.hint: Think about a manager who used to juggle two very different product ranges and now only has one.
steps.pre: So splitting the business can bring

steps.q: Before the split there was one HR team and one finance team for the whole business. After the split, each new company needs its own HR and finance team. What happens to the total number of these support staff needed?
steps.right: It rises, because each part now needs its own team
steps.wrong: It falls, because each part is now smaller
steps.hint: Two separate companies each need their own support functions, even though before there was only one.
steps.pre: So some roles are now repeated across both firms, creating

steps.q: Some workers now do better-focused, more secure jobs in a leaner firm, but other workers' roles are copied across both new firms. Overall, are workers guaranteed to be better off after a demerger?
steps.right: No, some may benefit while others may lose their jobs
steps.wrong: Yes, every worker ends up better off
steps.hint: Weigh up the renewed focus against the duplicated roles you just worked through.

steps.q: Before the split, one company sold both clothing and furniture, so a customer could sometimes get a discount for buying both together. After the split, the two companies operate separately. Can customers still combine both product ranges under one deal as easily?
steps.right: No, the combined range and bundled deals are gone
steps.wrong: Yes, nothing changes for what customers can buy
steps.hint: Think about what a customer could do when both products were sold by the same company.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: On the other hand, each demerged firm now focuses fully on one product, and (unlike when regulators step in to stop mergers as in horizontal integration cases) more separate firms are now competing for customers. Could this make consumers better off in some ways even as their combined deals disappear?
steps.right: Yes, sharper focus and more competition can improve service or prices
steps.wrong: No, consumers can only ever lose out from a demerger
steps.hint: Consider both the loss of bundled deals and the gain from firms specialising and competing harder.
